explain.headline: Supreme Court Ruling on Yes Bank AT-1 Bonds Highlights Need for Legal Compliance
static: Additional Tier-1 (AT-1) bonds are unsecured, perpetual bonds issued by banks to augment their core equity capital under Basel III norms.
AT-1 bonds have loss-absorption features, meaning they can be written down or converted to equity if a bank's capital falls below a specified threshold.
Under conventional corporate finance loss hierarchy, equity shareholders absorb losses before debt holders and bondholders when a firm faces distress.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is the primary banking regulator in India, operating under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 and the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
The Financial Resolution and Deposit Insurance (FRDI) Bill was introduced in Parliament in 2017 to provide a comprehensive resolution framework for financial institutions before being withdrawn.
Bespoke bank reconstructions in India have historically relied on powers under Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, enabling the central government to formulate schemes.
explain.what: The Supreme Court upheld the Bombay High Court verdict setting aside the write-down of Yes Bank's AT-1 bonds worth Rs 8,415 crore, ruling that the action lacked legal backing and due process.
explain.why_in_news: The Supreme Court delivered its verdict after four years, 23 hearings, and six bench changes following appeals by the RBI and Yes Bank.
explain.background: During Yes Bank's 2020 RBI-orchestrated rescue, AT-1 bonds were written down entirely while equity shareholders were left untouched, triggering a legal challenge over loss-absorption hierarchies and administrator powers.
significance: It reinforces that regulatory interventions during financial crises must strictly adhere to statutory powers and due process.
It exposes gaps in India's legal framework for financial distress and highlights the urgency of a comprehensive bank resolution law.
It reassures investors and mutual funds that contractual rights and regulatory predictability will be upheld during bank restructurings.

texts.x: The Supreme Court's Yes Bank AT-1 bonds verdict highlights gaps in India's bank resolution framework and the need for clear legal powers and investor safeguards.

points: The Supreme Court ruled in favour of investors whose Additional Tier-1 (AT-1) bonds worth Rs 8,415 crore were written down to zero during Yes Bank's 2020 reconstruction.
The ruling upheld the Bombay High Court decision, legally restoring the AT-1 bonds onto Yes Bank's balance sheet while noting equity shareholders were spared.
The author argues that the write-down inverted the conventional hierarchy of loss absorption, where equity shareholders normally bear losses before bondholders.
The Supreme Court based its decision on three legal infirmities: the final government notification did not authorise the write-down despite being in the draft.
The Court rejected the RBI-appointed administrator's reliance on general residuary powers since the reconstruction scheme did not expressly confer write-down authority.
The Court also noted that under the information memorandum, only Yes Bank could exercise the write-down power before the reconstruction scheme notification.
The judgment highlights that extraordinary regulatory interventions require clear statutory powers, proper authority, and a legally defensible process.
The authors call for a comprehensive financial resolution law to replace bespoke interventions and provide predictability for investors.

S ix years after Yes Bank’s reconstruction, the Supreme Court has ruled in favour of investors whose additional tier (AT-1) bonds were written down to zero, even as the bank’s equity shareholders were spared. Upholding the Bombay High Court’s decision, the court set aside the administrator’s action, legally restoring AT1 bonds worth Rs 8,415 crore onto Yes Bank’s balance sheet. The judgment has three implications for bank resolution in India. It underscores the importance of due process even during a financial crisis, clarifies the limits of powers exercised by RBI-appointed administrators, and exposes the inadequacy of India’s legal framework for resolving financial distress. In 2020, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) orchestrated a consortium-led recapitalisation of Yes Bank, which had been weakened by mismanagement and excessive exposures. These AT1 bonds were held largely by mutual funds, high-net-worth individuals, and other investors. points: The Constitution 131st Amendment Bill and the Delimitation Bill 2026 propose increasing Lok Sabha strength from 550 to 850 members to address heavy voter loads per constituency.
The core concern is that merely increasing members without expanding sitting hours or floor time will leave MPs muted and unable to represent citizens effectively.
India currently has 97.98 crore voters, resulting in a heavy load averaging roughly 18 lakh voters per Lok Sabha seat.
Constituencies feature stark disparities, ranging from 37.8 lakh voters in Malkajgiri to just 57,953 in Lakshadweep.
Question Hour suffers severely, functioning for only 60 percent of scheduled time in the 17th Lok Sabha and a mere 9 minutes during the Monsoon Session 2026.
With more MPs and unchanged hours, mechanisms like Question Hour, Zero Hour, and Private Members Business will lose their purpose due to intense sharing of limited slots.
Parliamentary productivity has declined sharply, with the 17th Lok Sabha averaging only 55 sitting days a year against 127 in the 1950s.
Legislative quality has dropped, as 35 percent of Bills in the 17th Lok Sabha passed with under an hour of discussion and only 17 percent went to standing committees.
Proposed reforms include statutory sitting time, amending Article 85 to mandate minimum working days, protecting question time, and introducing fixed Opposition days.
sum.text:
The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill and the Delimitation Bill, 2026 , introduced together, would raise the Lok Sabha’s strength from 550 to 850 members. The plan tackles the size of constituencies but not Parliament’s working capacity , so more members would share the same limited floor time , the hours the House sits to debate.
Two layers of representation: Voters need access to their Member of Parliament (MP) , and the MP needs floor time to speak for them. More MPs without more time is like more students in an unchanged class period.
Why delimitation is proposed: Delimitation redraws constituencies. India’s 97.98 crore voters give each Lok Sabha seat roughly 18 lakh voters, a heavy load for one MP.
Uneven constituencies: Malkajgiri in Telangana has 37.8 lakh voters. Lakshadweep has just 57,953 .
The takeaway: More seats without more floor time would leave representatives “muted on the floor” .
Question Hour: Question Hour is the sitting time when MPs question Ministers. Lok Sabha rules allow at most 20 starred questions (answered orally) and 230 unstarred questions (answered in writing) per sitting day.
Daily ballot: Each MP can submit up to five questions a day, but a ballot picks only a tiny fraction for answer.
Lower odds at 850: With more MPs and unchanged sitting hours, an MP’s chance of an oral answer from a Minister falls further.
17th Lok Sabha record: Question Hour functioned for only 60% of its scheduled time.
Monsoon Session 2026: Question Hour ran for only 1% of scheduled time, nine minutes in all. More members cannot improve executive-legislative accountability , Ministers answering to Parliament, if the hour does not run.
Zero Hour: MPs use it to raise urgent issues without advance notice. Eg. Regional crop failures or disaster relief.
Private Members’ Business: It lets MPs who are not Ministers bring in their own Bills.
Unprotected instruments: With more MPs sharing the same slots, these tools lose their purpose unless rules protect the time to use them.
Article 85(1): The President summons each House at such time and place as he thinks fit. Six months must not pass between one session’s last sitting and the next session’s first.
No minimum days: The Article caps the gap between sessions but fixes no minimum number of sitting days, so the government of the day sets the calendar.

The IDBI strategic disinvestment , the largest FDI in India’s financial sector, carries a broader significance. The cabinet’s decision to divest it to a private entity, Fairfax, is a major step toward improving the efficiency of financial intermediation. It could signal lower capital costs. Even so, it will be a long haul.
The arc of capital reform has come full circle: From nationalising private banks to privatising a national bank. This matters because India’s cost of capital remains above that of ASEAN peers, weakening competitiveness. Within the domestic regulatory framework, the legacy burden of the cash-reserve ratio, statutory liquidity ratio and priority-sector lending circumscribes optimum credit allocation. A banking system steeped in PSU culture may not consistently give Indian entrepreneurs capital at a globally competitive cost.
In the past, I have lamented the tardy pace of reforms in India’s factors of production (land, labour, capital) despite the big changes of 1991. Lomborg claimed India must spend 4% of GDP annually for half a century on net zero, totaling $8.1 tn, which he said diverts funds from health and education.

Green investments like solar plants and EVs are revenue-earning assets mostly financed by private and foreign capital, not government budgets.
Lomborg misquoted a Lancet Planetary Health study on heat versus cold deaths and dismissed the heavy economic costs of rising heat.
A 2024 Lancet Countdown estimate shows India lost 247 bn potential labour hours to heat, causing a $194 bn income loss largely in agriculture and construction.

But data he quotes and reports he cites reach almost the opposite conclusion. NITI Aayog's study, 'Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero', estimates that net zero needs $8.1 tn additional investment over the next 45 yrs. Lomborg divides this by today's GDP and concludes that India must spend 4% of GDP every year for half a century to achieve net zero, more than it spends on education or health. This is fakery, not analysis. The $8.1 tn is spent in an economy projected to grow to $30 tn by 2047, and keep growing thereafter. So, cumulatively, additional investment comes to 0.8% of GDP, 70% of which is required after 2050. Lomborg's '4%' would be correct only if India stopped growing after 2025. 135054371 Similarly, his comparison of net-zero investments with schools and hospitals equates apples with oranges. $8.1 tn is capex on solar, EVs and green steel, assets that earn revenue, most of them financed by banks, private capital and foreign investors, not by government budgets. A solar plant pays for itself, a primary school doesn't - and shouldn't. Claiming that a rupee of private capital is a rupee taken from a child's classroom is intellectual dishonesty. Worse, he has got his arithmetic wrong. Even if India's spending on health and education stays at today's share of GDP till 2070, the additional net-zero investment is at most ¼th of either. So, his claim of net zero seizing money from health and education is false. He applies the same sleight of hand to every number he touches. Heat, he says, kills fewer than 90,000 Indians a year, while cold kills more than 6 lakh. So, concern about rising heat is misplaced. The Supreme Court has declared access to and use of the internet a fundamental right of children and directed the Centre to create a national database to detect and remove sexually explicit visual content depicting minors from digital platforms, news agency Press Trust of India reported.
The court issued the order while hearing a petition highlighting an alarming increase in child sexual exploitation and abuse material, or CSEAM, circulating on social media platforms. It also issued several directions aimed at curbing the rise of such content on social media and other online platforms.
A bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran said the internet was the marketplace of ideas, creative expression and information. Its value lay not only in the information it contained but also in the access it provided to adults and children, the bench said.
"In view of the foregoing, we have no hesitation in saying that the right to access and use the internet is a fundamental right of every individual under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. Our children, irrespective of their age, enjoy the same rights, and to deny the same altogether would be as absurd as saying children below a certain age do not have a conscience worth protecting or a freedom of speech worth expressing," the court said in its 137-page order passed on October 15.

The court said its observations did not mean that age-based restrictions should be ruled out. "We acknowledge that some form of safeguards are necessary for the safety of our children online and the moderation of the content accessible at their fingertips," it said.

New Delhi, October 19 (IANS): The Union Finance Ministry's Department of Financial Services (DFS) is organising a nationwide campaign for the saturation of financial inclusion schemes and other key interventions at the gram panchayat and urban local body level starting this week. The campaign will run from October 21 to December 31, covering 2.70 lakh gram panchayats and urban local bodies in the country, according to a Finance Ministry statement issued on Monday. During this period, banks will conduct camps for enrolments under the Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY), the Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY), and the Atal Pension Yojana (APY). Enrolment under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana to support the objective of saturation of KCC accounts for the upcoming Rabi season will also take place as part of the financial inclusion drive. The campaign reflects the government’s commitment to empowering citizens at the last mile and building a more inclusive society by bringing them into the formal financial system. A preparatory meeting with senior management of Banks and SLBC was held today under the chairmanship of the Joint Secretary, Financial Inclusion, Department of Finance. The progress under the campaign will be closely monitored by key stakeholders including the state administration, banks and the Department of Finance, the statement added.

New Delhi, Oct 19 (IANS) India's semiconductor ecosystem is steadily taking shape with 12 approved projects across six states, backed by more than Rs 1.64 lakh crore in committed investments, former NITI Aayog CEO and G20 Sherpa Amitabh Kant said on Monday.
Sharing a graphic titled "The New Semiconductor Map of India" on social media platform X, Kant said the country's semiconductor future is taking shape through a growing network of fabrication, packaging, testing, and advanced technology facilities.
"6 states and 12 approved projects, backed by Rs 1.64 lakh crore+ in committed investments. India’s semiconductor future is taking shape!" he stated.
Gujarat has emerged as the biggest hub for semiconductor investments. The state hosts six approved projects, including the Tata-PSMC semiconductor fabrication plant at Dholera with an investment of Rs 91,526 crore and a planned capacity of more than 50,000 wafers per month.
Other major projects in the state include Micron Technology's DRAM and NAND assembly and test facility at Sanand with an investment of Rs 22,516 crore, and the CG Power-Renesas-Stars semiconductor OSAT facility involving Rs 7,584 crore of investment.
The state is also home to facilities being developed by Kaynes Semicon, Crystal Matrix, and Suchi Semicon, covering semiconductor packaging, compound semiconductors, mini-LED technologies, and discrete semiconductor manufacturing.
In Assam, Tata Semiconductor Assembly and Test is setting up an OSAT and packaging facility involving an investment of Rs 27,120 crore with a proposed capacity of around 48 million units per day.
Odisha has secured two projects. SiCSem is developing a silicon carbide fabrication and packaging facility with an investment of Rs 2,066 crore, while 3D Glass Solutions is establishing an advanced packaging and 3D integration project with an investment of Rs 1,943 crore.
Andhra Pradesh is hosting an Advanced System in Package (ASIP) facility focused on system-in-package technologies with an investment of about Rs 480 crore and a proposed capacity of nearly 96 million units annually.
Punjab is also part of the emerging semiconductor ecosystem, with CDIL setting up a power semiconductor project involving an investment of Rs 117 crore.

Understanding Stampede: It’s Really a Crowd Crush What is loosely called a “stampede” is more accurately a crowd crush — a situation where crowd density becomes so high that individuals lose control over their own movement. Structural Causes: Weak temporary structures, inadequate barricades, poorly lit stairways, narrow entry/exit points. Trigger Events: Fires, electrical failures, security scares, or failures of crowd management.
Critical NDMA Insight: Deaths usually result not from literal “trampling” but from compressive asphyxia — when people packed tightly together cannot expand their chest to breathe. Preliminary accounts suggest multiple risk factors converged: Heavy pandal-hopper crowds when rain began suddenly. People moving forward as some fell, with the crowd behind continuing to press ahead.
A Public Address (PA) system announcement that may have intensified the rush. static: Section 125A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, penalises candidates for failing to furnish information or giving false information in nomination affidavits.
Section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) places restrictions on courts taking direct cognisance of certain offences without a formal complaint by a public servant.

explain.why_in_news: The Supreme Court settled this question while hearing an appeal against a Karnataka High Court order that had quashed a voter's complaint against an MLA.
explain.background: Section 195 CrPC bars courts from taking direct cognisance of certain offences without a public servant's written complaint, but the Supreme Court clarified that this restriction does not apply to offences under Section 125A of the RP Act.

points: The Supreme Court held that a private complaint can be filed under the Representation of the People Act to probe candidates for false declarations in nomination affidavits.
A bench led by Justice Dipankar Datta overruled a Karnataka High Court order requiring such complaints to satisfy Section 195 of the CrPC.
The core issue debated was whether Section 125A of the RP Act must pass through the rigours of Section 195 CrPC, which restricts direct cognisance by magistrates.
The Supreme Court ruled that Section 195 CrPC only bars cognisance of specified offences, primarily Sections 171 to 188 of the erstwhile IPC, and does not mention Section 125A of the RP Act.
The bench noted that Section 125A was added in 2002 and Section 195 CrPC was amended in 2006, making the legislative omission deliberate.
The court stated that magistrates are empowered to deal with frivolous or harassing complaints through judicial scrutiny, preventing the misuse of provisions.
Despite clarifying the legal position in favor of private complaints, the Supreme Court upheld the quashing of the specific complaint against the MLA as the allegations were effectively rebutted.
The ruling strengthens voter-led enforcement of candidate disclosures and reinforces transparency principles established in earlier judgments.

A bench led by Justice Dipankar Datta overruled a Karnataka High Court order, which said that a complaint alleging an offence under section 125A of the RP Act needs to satisfy section 195 of the criminal procedure code (CrPC). Section 195 of CrPC restricts criminal courts (magistrate) from taking direct cognisance of certain specific offences unless a written complaint is formally filed by a designated public servant or the concerned court. The fifth edition of the India-Australia Joint Military Exercise AUSTRAHIND 2026 commenced on Monday at the Foreign Training Node in Thiruvananthapuram, Keralam, with around 120 personnel each from the Indian Army and the Australian Army participating in the exercise.
The exercise, scheduled till November 1, aims to enhance interoperability, jointmanship, and operational coordination between the two armies, with a focus on joint operations in island and coastal environments.
The Indian Army contingent comprises troops from the Garhwal Rifles, along with personnel from other arms and services, while the Australian Army contingent comprises troops from the 13 Brigade, according to a press release by the Ministry of Defence.
During the exercise, troops from both armies will undertake joint planning, tactical drills and combat-oriented training under realistic operational conditions, including aerial and maritime dimensions. The training will focus on coordinated operations in coastal and island environments, surveillance and reconnaissance, protection of vital installations, and responses to Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) contingencies. The exercise will also facilitate the exchange of professional experience and best practices between the participating forces.
For the first time, an observer delegation from New Zealand will also participate in the exercise.
The exercise will be conducted under the theme “Joint Sub-Conventional Operations in Island and Coastal Environment under Chapter VII of the UN Mandate”. It aims to develop a common understanding of tactics, techniques, and procedures for operations in island and coastal terrain while strengthening interoperability and coordination between the two armies.

The Union environment ministry, in an affidavit, has said this is due to the state repeatedly failing to provide the information required to take the process forward and has issued at least three reminders since July last year to the state to share it. The affidavit, dated October 5 and submitted before the National Green Tribunal (NGT) said without complete information, the process to notify the ESZ could not be dispensed with or bypassed. The draft notification to declare an ESZ around the Similipal Tiger Reserve and the Hadgarh Wildlife Sanctuary was issued on January 29, 2019. The affidavit details the correspondence between the Centre and Odisha over the past few years. sum.text:
The Karnataka High Court has ruled that criticising a Supreme Court judgment by calling it a “denial of justice” does not, by itself, amount to a criminal offence. The court quashed a First Information Report (FIR) registered against 13 people accused of painting slogans on a public wall questioning an apex court verdict, underlining the importance of the right to dissent in a democracy.
Wall slogans questioning Supreme Court verdict led to FIR
The case originated in 2019 when slogans criticising a Supreme Court judgment were allegedly painted on roadside walls in Mangaluru. According to the police complaint, the slogans described the verdict as a “denial of justice” and called for raising a “voice for justice”.
The police alleged that the slogans were associated with the Popular Front of India (PFI) and could create disharmony. Following a suo motu complaint by an Assistant Sub-Inspector at Maangaluru South Police Station, an FIR was registered against 13 people.
The accused approached the High Court, arguing that the allegations did not establish the ingredients of the offences invoked against them. The FIR included charges under Sections 153A and 295A of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), along with criminal conspiracy under Section 120B and provisions of the Karnataka Open Place Disfigurement Act, 1951.
Their counsel argued that expressing disagreement with a judicial verdict cannot automatically be treated as promoting enmity or outraging religious feelings. The petitioners also relied on constitutional protections for freedom of speech and expression.
Court says criticism alone does not establish an offence
Justice H.P. Sandesh observed that the words cited in the complaint did not satisfy the requirements of Sections 153A and 295A of the IPC. The court noted that Section 153A requires more than mere disagreement or criticism. Assessing whether speech promotes enmity involves considering its general impact on a significant number of reasonable people.
How the right to dissent shaped the verdict
Relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Javed Ahmad Hajam v. State of Maharashtra, the High Court reiterated that lawful dissent is protected under Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution.
The court concluded that the slogans expressed dissatisfaction with the judgment and called for justice, without meeting the legal threshold for the alleged offences. It therefore exercised its powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash the proceedings.

points: The Allahabad High Court questioned the Uttar Pradesh Dedicated Backward Classes Commission regarding its survey methodology for determining OBC reservations in panchayat polls.
Rural body elections in Uttar Pradesh have been delayed because the state government failed to complete the required empirical survey on OBC representation on time.
The core issue involves ensuring that the commission conducts a rigorous, contemporaneous empirical investigation to satisfy the Supreme Court's 'triple test' conditions.
The five-member commission, led by retired high court judge Ram Autar Singh, stated that 60% of data collection covering 40 districts has been completed.
On October 9, a division bench noted that very few individuals appeared before the commission in districts like Agra, highlighting gaps in obtaining representative data.
In Agra, only 179 out of over 3 lakh OBC residents appeared, and statements were recorded from just 29 individuals, failing to cover even those present.
The high court also observed that an advisory committee constituted for the panel had not held a single meeting until October 12, five months after formation.
The court directed the commission to submit a comprehensive statement detailing its work in Agra, its caste-wise data collection, and its final assessment methodology.
sum.text:
New Delhi: In May, in compliance with mandatory requirements laid down by the Supreme Court for local body polls, the Yogi Adityanath cabinet approved the formation of the Uttar Pradesh Dedicated Backward Classes Commission to determine reservations for Other Backward Classes (OBCs) in three-tier Panchayati Raj institutions. Panchayat or rural body polls in the state have been held up this time as the government has not been able to conduct on time an empirical survey to evaluate OBC representation. With over 12 crore voters (in the 2021 and 2026 elections), the rural body elections in UP are one of the largest elections conducted in the country.
Five months after the five-member commission led by retired Allahabad high court judge Ram Autar Singh started the exercise, the Allahabad high court has flagged several questions regarding the manner in which it is being conducted. The court, which is currently hearing a batch of petitions from individuals seeking timely panchayat polls, has on several occasions questioned the state on the underlying cause for the delay. The Uttar Pradesh Dedicated Backward Classes Commission last week informed the court that 60% of the data collection work has been completed, covering 40 districts.
It assured the bench that the remaining 40%, pertaining to the remaining districts, will also be completed soon. On October 9, a division bench of Justices Ajit Kumar and Garima Prashad pointed out that according to records submitted by the commission, the number of persons who appeared before it on scheduled meeting dates was far fewer than required to obtain requisite, representative data. Official notices had been published in widely circulated daily newspapers, and questionnaires were issued to individuals who approached the commission during its visits to various districts.
However, the judges observed that in Agra, for example, despite the public notices issued, only a very small number of persons – just 179 out of a total district OBC population exceeding 3 lakh – appeared before the commission. Furthermore, even though questionnaires were issued to all present, statements were recorded from only 29 individuals, failing to cover even the small group of 179 who showed up. The commission is tasked with conducting a contemporary, continuous empirical investigation and study into the nature and effects of backwardness to enable proportional, body-wise reservations for identified OBC populations in three-tier Panchayat bodies.
